subject: english
name: English
exam: Basic Education Examination (BEE), grade 8. The CDC basic-level assessment scheme gives continuous (internal) assessment 50 % weight and the external written paper 50 %; the local level (palika) conducts and marks it. English has no Group A/B/C paper: the paper tests reading comprehension, grammar and writing, so the practice sets here use reading, grammar and writing sections with full answer keys.

units.title: A Tour to Central Zoo / A Request Letter

A request letter: purpose, politeness and layout

Writing: interpreting a timetable and a schedule; filling in a form

sections.title: A Tour to Central Zoo
A Request Letter
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit
Reading for different purposes

summary: The Central Zoo is in Jawalakhel, Lalitpur; it opened in 1932 and is now run by the National Trust for Nature Conservation.
A timetable is read in three steps: find the row, find the column, read the meeting cell.
The present simple tense is used for facts, habits and timetables: the zoo opens at ten.
can = ability or a direct request; could = a polite request or past ability; would = the most polite request.
A modal verb never takes -s and is always followed by the bare verb.
A formal letter needs the sender's address, the date, the receiver's address, the salutation, a subject line, the body, the closing and the signature.
Yours faithfully follows Dear Sir; Yours sincerely follows a name.
A request letter must give details — the date, the time and the number of people — and must not sound like an order.

units.title: A Father's Letter to his Son / Poem: Changing
topics: A letter of advice: tone, point of view and structure
Poetry: theme, speaker and the idea of personal change
Grammar: yes/no questions
Writing: completing a skeleton story; writing an e-mail
Project work: composing a poem; pronunciation: /t/, /d/, /ɪd/

sections.title: A Father's Letter to his Son
Poem: Changing
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit

summary: A letter of advice is warm and personal: it uses the first person, begins with a shared memory and ends by handing responsibility to the reader.
Its structure is memory → advice → trust, and its tone is encouraging, never scolding.
A poem has a speaker (the voice), a theme (the idea it returns to) and images (the pictures that make the idea visible).
The theme of "Changing" is that change is unavoidable and can be accepted.
A yes/no question begins with a helping verb; if there is none, use do, does or did.
A short answer repeats the helping verb: Yes, he does. Not Yes, he.
A skeleton story is planned in four moves: setting, problem, attempts, resolution — and written in one tense.
An e-mail needs a subject line, a greeting, short body paragraphs, a closing and a signature.

units.title: Public Announcements / How to Wash Clothes in a Washing Machine
topics: Announcements: the language of notice-giving
Instructions and the sequence of steps
Grammar: reported speech — yes/no questions
Writing: writing an announcement; preparing a set of instructions
Pronunciation: /r/

sections.title: Public Announcements
How to Wash Clothes in a Washing Machine
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit
The language of instructions

summary: An announcement gives one piece of information in a hurry and answers what, where, when, who and what to do.
It has a heading, the information, the action and the issuer — and no greeting or closing.
Instructions use the imperative and must be in the correct order, because each step depends on the one before it.
Reported yes/no questions are joined with if or whether, lose the question mark and use statement word order.
Reported speech moves the tense one step back and changes the pronoun and the time words.
The letter r is pronounced when a vowel follows it (red, road) and is silent when it is at the end of a word or before a consonant (car, park in standard British English).

units.title: A Memoir: A Visit to Mustang / A Diary Entry
topics: Memoir and diary as records of personal experience
Descriptive writing about a place and an event
Grammar: present perfect and past simple
Writing: an account of a memorable event; a diary entry
Pronunciation: diphthongs

sections.title: A Memoir: A Visit to Mustang
A Diary Entry
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit
Writing a memoir and a diary: the difference

summary: A memoir is a first-person account written after the event, which ends with what the experience meant to the writer.
A diary entry is written on the day, keeps one day in view and ends with a feeling.
Mustang is the trans-Himalayan district of Nepal; the Kali Gandaki has cut one of the world's deepest gorges between the Annapurna and Dhaulagiri ranges.
The valley lies in a rain shadow, so it is dry while southern Nepal is wet.
Lo Manthang, Kagbeni and Muktinath are on the route; Thakali, Gurung, Magar and Bhotiya people live in the district.
Describing a place well uses more than sight: hearing, smell, touch and feeling.
Past simple = a finished action at a finished time; present perfect = an experience or a result whose time is not stated and which is still relevant now.
Time words decide the tense: yesterday goes with the past simple; ever, never, just, yet, since, for go with the present perfect.

units.title: The Old Woman and the Lime Tree / Poem: Free Birds
topics: Narrative fiction: plot, character and message
Poetry: freedom as a theme; imagery
Grammar: reported speech — imperatives; punctuation
Writing: completing a skeleton story
Project work: collecting the expressions used for persuading

sections.title: The Old Woman and the Lime Tree
Poem: Free Birds
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit

summary: A folk tale was told aloud before it was written; it is short, has few characters, often uses a rule of three, and ends with a message.
Every plot has five stages: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.
Describe a character from what they do, not from what you feel about them.
The theme of the story is the relationship between a person and a living thing that cannot speak for itself; the message is proved by the climax.
"Free Birds" shows, through contrast between the cage and the sky, that freedom is worth more than safety.
Reported imperatives use told / asked / warned + object + to + verb, and not to for negatives.
In direct speech the quotation takes a capital letter, the comma goes after the reporting clause, and the full stop or question mark goes inside the quotation marks.

units.title: Traditional Wedding Customs around the World / Life Saving Inventions
topics: Descriptive writing about ceremonies and customs
Expository writing about inventions and their effect
Grammar: causative verbs; subject–verb agreement
Writing: describing a ceremony; paraphrasing
Project work: making a collage; pronunciation: /s/, /z/, /ɪz/

sections.title: Traditional Wedding Customs around the World
Life Saving Inventions
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit

summary: Expository writing explains; descriptive-comparative writing sets several things side by side and explains each one.
Every wedding custom can be described by answering: what is done, why, and what it symbolises.
Weddings everywhere contain a promise, a feast and a procession.
Cause-and-effect writing names the problem, the invention and the effect.
Vaccination, antiseptics, antibiotics and ORS are four inventions that together saved more lives than any other group of inventions in history.
The cheapest life savers reached the most people.
Causative: have / get + object + past participle (I had my hair cut).
make / let / help take a bare verb or to + verb: made me sit, let me go, helped me carry.

units.title: Weather Forecast / Migration
topics: The language of weather forecasting and prediction
Migration: causes, kinds and effects
Grammar: future simple, going to future and future perfect
Writing: paragraphs on the environment
Project work: designing a picture; punctuation

sections.title: Weather Forecast
Migration
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit
Reading a weather forecast

summary: A weather forecast is predictive writing; its may, likely and expected tell you how confident the forecaster is.
Nepali forecasts are regional because the Tarai, the hills and the Himalaya have different climates at the same moment.
Migration is the movement of people to live in another place; internal migration stays inside the country, international migration crosses a border.
Push factors drive people out; pull factors attract them in.
Remittances are a large part of Nepal's economy, but migration also empties fields and closes village schools.
Birds migrate on the same routes each year, for food and for breeding.
will = prediction or a decision made now; going to = a plan already made; present continuous = an arrangement; present simple = a timetable.
Future perfect (will have + past participle) = finished before a stated future time.

units.title: Having Fun / Historical Inventions
topics: Talking about the past in narration
Historical inventions and their importance
Grammar: past simple, past continuous and past perfect; used to
Writing: completing a skeleton story; a narrative essay
Project work: making a survey; pronunciation of the past tense endings

sections.title: Having Fun
Historical Inventions
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit

summary: Leisure is the time left after work, school and sleep; how people spend it shows how much space, money and daylight they have.
Older Nepali leisure was shared, public and cheap; modern leisure is often private, indoor and paid for.
Radio, television, migration to cities and the mobile phone changed that pattern within two generations.
Historical writing about an invention must always answer "so what?" — what changed for ordinary people.
The printing press, the steam engine, electric light, the telephone and radio, and the computer all made something cheaper or faster, moved activity to a new place, and changed the daily routine.
Past simple = finished action; past continuous = in progress; past perfect = the earlier of two past actions.
used to describes a past habit that has stopped; after did, write use to, with no -d.

units.title: The Leap between High School and College / Smartphones in our Life
topics: Making comparison and contrast in writing
Advantages and disadvantages of technology
Grammar: comparative and superlative; adverbs of degree
Writing: a paragraph comparing places; an essay on technology
Pronunciation: college-related words

sections.title: The Leap between High School and College
Smartphones in our Life
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit
Talking about technology: useful vocabulary

summary: School and college differ in supervision, breadth, the contact between teacher and student, and the freedom given.
The students who find the leap hardest are those who were supervised the most closely in school.
A discursive essay presents advantages, then disadvantages, then a balanced conclusion.
A smartphone is a telephone, library, market, bank and classroom at once — and also a source of distraction, cost and lost privacy.
Comparative compares two things (cheaper than); superlative compares three or more (the cheapest).
Irregulars: good → better → best; bad → worse → worst; far → further → furthest.
Never use more with -er, and never use very before a comparative — use much or far.
Adverbs of degree: slightly, quite, rather, very, extremely, almost, nearly.

units.title: Vacancy Announcement / Invitation
topics: Reading a job advertisement: the information it must give
Invitations: formal and informal; accepting and declining
Grammar: prepositions of place and time; question tags
Writing: a vacancy advertisement; a message of invitation
Project work: designing an invitation card; pronunciation of -tion and -sion

sections.title: Vacancy Announcement
Invitation
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit
Vocabulary of announcements and invitations

summary: A vacancy announcement is a formal public notice; it must give the post, the employer, the qualification, the duties, the pay, the method of application, the deadline and the contact.
The qualification and the deadline decide who can apply.
An invitation may be formal or informal; a formal one ends with an R.S.V.P. line asking for a reply.
at a point of time, on a day or date, in a month, year or enclosed space.
by = not later than; until = up to then; for = a length of time; since = from a point in the past until now.
A question tag repeats the helping verb, flips the polarity, and uses a pronoun: You are coming, aren't you?

units.title: Sir Isaac Newton / Khaptad National Park
topics: Biography: the life and work of a scientist
Describing a place: location, features and importance
Grammar: relative clauses; articles
Writing: preparing a leaflet; writing a set of rules
Project work: collecting information about a place; tongue twisters

sections.title: Sir Isaac Newton
Khaptad National Park
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit

summary: A biography tells a real person's life in time order and explains the connection between its periods.
Isaac Newton (1642–1727) worked out the binomial theorem, calculus and the composition of white light during the plague years of 1665–66, and published the Principia in 1687.
The apple story stands for the insight that one force — gravitation — governs both a falling apple and the orbit of the Moon.
A place description answers: where, what it is like, what lives there and why it matters.
Khaptad National Park (est. 1984, about 225 km²) is in the far west of Nepal, and is famous for its open plateau grassland, wild flowers, medicinal herbs and the hermitage of Khaptad Baba.
Relative clauses use who, which, that, whose, where, when and sit immediately after the noun they describe.
Use a/an by sound, the for something specific or unique, and no article for plurals and uncountable nouns used generally.

units.title: Nepal's Bird Man / Poem: My Teacher Ate my Homework
topics: A profile of a conservationist, and the work of bird conservation in Nepal
Humorous poetry: exaggeration and rhyme
Grammar: verb + -ing and infinitive; yes/no and wh questions
Writing: an essay on hobbies and interests
Project work: collecting a poem; pronunciation of words with -ch

sections.title: Nepal's Bird Man
Poem: My Teacher Ate my Homework
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit

summary: A profile explains what a living person does: the problem, the work, the result and the difficulty.
Conservation is counting, protecting habitat, working with people and teaching — not only sentiment.
Nepal has recorded more than 850 bird species and lies on a migratory flyway, so its wetlands matter far beyond its borders.
The veterinary drug diclofenac caused a collapse in South Asian vultures; the ban in 2006 and the safe feeding sites are the remedy.
Humorous verse works by exaggeration, rhyme and a punch line.
enjoy, finish, mind, avoid, practise, suggest take the -ing form.
want, decide, hope, plan, try, promise, learn take to + verb.
make, let, see, hear, watch take the bare verb.

units.title: Nepal is the First Country to Double its Tiger Population / Drama: A Mousetrap
topics: Reading and interpreting charts, graphs and tables
Drama: plot, characters and stage directions
Grammar: much/many, some/any; expressing quantity
Writing: writing a description of data; presenting data in a graph
Pronunciation: words used to interpret charts and graphs

sections.title: Nepal is the First Country to Double its Tiger Population
Drama: A Mousetrap
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit
Writing about data and conservation

summary: Nepal was the first of the thirteen tiger-range countries to double its wild tiger population under the TX2 target set in 2010.
The estimates rose from about 121 tigers in 2009 to about 355 in 2022.
The figures come from the National Tiger and Prey Survey, which identifies individual tigers by their unique stripe patterns in camera-trap photographs.
The increase followed the linking of protected areas, the restoration of prey and grassland, and the suppression of poaching.
The success brings a new problem: tigers need large territories, so a growing population presses against the parks' boundaries.
A drama is written to be performed; the audience learns about characters from dialogue and stage directions, not from a narrator.
A data description gives the overall trend first, then the figures, then the turning point, then the conclusion.
many with countable plurals; much with uncountables; some in positives; any in negatives and questions; a few / a little = some, few / little = almost none.

units.title: The Magic Mirror / Poem: If I was a Superhero
topics: Folk tale and wish-fulfilment narrative
Poetry: the conditional and the imagination
Grammar: second conditional; adjectives and adverbs
Writing: writing a folk tale; a description of an imaginary event
Pronunciation: British and American differences

sections.title: The Magic Mirror
Poem: If I was a Superhero
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit
Writing a story: dialogue and description together

summary: A magic-object folk tale uses the object to test a character: the magic makes the choice possible, the character makes it.
A moral must be stated in one sentence and proved by one moment in the story.
A conditional poem imagines what the speaker would do if something impossible were true; the choice, not the power, is the point.
Poems use repetition for rhythm, hyperbole for effect and a twist at the end.
First conditional: If + present, will + verb — a real possibility.
Second conditional: If + past, would + verb — imaginary or unlikely; use were with be in written English.
Third conditional: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle — impossible, because the moment has passed.
Adjectives describe nouns; adverbs describe verbs. good → well, fast → fast, hard → hard.

units.title: Conservation of Earth / An Official Notice
topics: Argumentative writing on conservation
Notices: purpose, audience and format
Grammar: connectives of reason, purpose and contrast
Writing: an argumentative essay; an official notice
Project work: preparing a bulletin board; English consonants

sections.title: Conservation of Earth
An Official Notice
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit
The language of persuasion

summary: An argumentative essay has four parts: position, reasons with evidence, counter-argument and call to action.
The main environmental problems in the text are over-consumption and emissions, the loss of forest and biodiversity, and waste.
Conservation is not the opposite of development: it protects the soil, water and forest that farming and tourism depend on.
An official notice names the office, carries the word NOTICE, a reference number and date, a subject line, the information, the action required and a signature block.
Reason: because, since, as; because of + noun.
Purpose: to, in order to, so as to, so that + clause.
Contrast: but, however, although, whereas, on the other hand. Never pair although with but.
Commas separate list items, follow an introductory clause, and precede but and so between full sentences.

units.title: An Anecdote: Why I Became a Vegan / A History of Pens
topics: Anecdote and personal narrative
Historical writing about an everyday object
Grammar: past simple, past continuous, past perfect
Writing: a story; paragraphs about historical events
Project work: describing major events; words with silent letters

sections.title: An Anecdote: Why I Became a Vegan
A History of Pens
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit
Writing from a personal angle: the anecdote

summary: An anecdote is a short account of one incident, told to explain a decision or make a point; it has a situation, a turning point, a consequence and a point.
The turning point should be described in more detail than anything else.
The text about veganism is not asking the reader to change diet; it is asking how much we want to know about what we depend on.
Historical writing about an object gives the problem, the earliest form, each improvement and the effect on ordinary people.
The pen's history runs: reed pen → quill → steel nib → fountain pen → ballpoint → felt-tip and stylus.
Each improvement answered a complaint about the previous pen.
Past continuous sets the scene, past simple carries the events, past perfect marks the earlier of two past actions.

units.title: Naresh and the Stranger / Poem: From a Railway Carriage
topics: Story: suspense, character and resolution
Poetry: rhythm and the scenery of a journey
Grammar: voice (active and passive)
Writing: an e-mail; a reply letter to an invitation
Project work: collecting expressions to make offers and to accept or decline

sections.title: Naresh and the Stranger
Poem: From a Railway Carriage
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit
Describing a journey: the language of narrative

summary: Suspense is the reader's uncertainty about what happens next, built by a stranger, a small doubt, limited information, delay and a false resolution.
A story about a trust decision is really a story about the character who has to make it.
"From a Railway Carriage" is by Robert Louis Stevenson (A Child's Garden of Verses, 1885); its short lines and paired rhymes imitate the sound of a train.
Its imagery is entirely visual, and its incompleteness is what conveys speed.
Active: the subject does the action. Passive: be + past participle, used when the doer is unknown or unimportant, or when the action matters more.
An e-mail has To, Subject, greeting, body, closing and signature.
A reply to an invitation must be definite — accepting with thanks, or declining with thanks and a brief reason.

units.title: Road Accidents in Nepal: Are Poor Roads Solely to Blame? / Poem: Long Life
topics: Discussion and opinion writing on a social problem
Poetry: the theme and the structure of the poem
Grammar: intensifiers (too, enough); subject–verb agreement
Writing: an opinion essay; punctuation
Project work: filling in a survey form and making a presentation

sections.title: Road Accidents in Nepal: Are Poor Roads Solely to Blame?
Poem: Long Life
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit

summary: A discussion essay takes a question, argues one side, argues the other, then weighs both.
Bad roads, driver behaviour, vehicle condition and weak enforcement act together; no single cause is solely to blame for road accidents.
Speeding, overtaking on bends, drinking and driving, fatigue and overloading are the main human causes.
Education is part of road safety, because pedestrians are involved too.
"Long Life" redefines its own title: a life is measured by how it is lived, not by how many years it lasts.
too + adjective means a problem; adjective + enough means sufficient; very means a high degree without a problem.
so + adjective + that and such a + noun + that express a degree with a result.
The number of takes a singular verb; a number of takes a plural; a phrase between subject and verb changes nothing.

units.title: A Tale of Two Birds / News Report: Pokhara International Airport Inaugurated
topics: Folk narrative and its moral
The newspaper report: headline, lead and body
Grammar: reported speech
Writing: a story; a news report
Project work: designing the front page of a newspaper; consonant clusters

sections.title: A Tale of Two Birds
News Report: Pokhara International Airport Inaugurated
Grammar and writing tasks of the unit
The news report, line by line

summary: A folk tale uses parallelism — the same situation twice with one thing changed — so that the reader makes the comparison without being told to.
The moral of "A Tale of Two Birds" is that we become like the company we keep and the words we hear.
A news report answers who, what, where, when, why and how in its opening paragraph, called the lead.
Pokhara Regional International Airport was inaugurated on 1 January 2023 by Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal; it is Nepal's second international airport.
Its runway is 2,500 m long, its terminal is designed for about a million passengers a year, and it was built by CAMC on a Chinese loan of about Rs 22 billion.
A good report gives both the hopes and the criticisms, without taking sides.
Reported speech changes the reporting verb, the tense, the pronoun and the time and place words; questions are joined with if or the question word; orders use told / asked / warned + to + verb.
News writing uses the passive and the past tense and never uses I.
